chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
title: Why he tuned down: blending with Doug Daniels's tiple
summary: He began tuning lower to blend with the high tiples, especially Doug's, and debates with Rosenberg whether it was half or whole step.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: When did you first start to tune down your guitar?
When you started playing with horns, or --
No. When I started playing with the tipples. I couldn't get that high with them tipples, because them tipples was high.
Right. So you wanted to get a little lower.
Yeah. I wanted to get lower.
Blend in, yeah. So he was playing a lot in B-flat and F?
Uh-huh. I see. I see. Somehow -
Everytime he'd play them keys, he'd have to change it. He'd change the notes.
Because he didn't know the key it was in until he changed the notes. He'd get it down to a natural note, he wanted to play it.

Then probably -- let me -- I'm just trying to reconstruct this, because you're the only one I know that plays -- you know, in all those recordings you do, particularly on an acoustic guitar, where you have the thing tuned a whole step low, you know?
It couldn't be a half step.
To For me, yeah. I don't know maybe it is for somebody else.
I mean down, so when you play a C chord --
Yeah. They tell me I'm doing it a half step lower.
That's what they said to me. I don't know.
The thing is I'd always thought that the reason you did that was because playing with clarinets and saxophones and so forth, they play a lot in the flat keys, you know.
They play a lot in B-flat, E-flat, F, and so forth.
I always figured, well that was hip because then you could play low down on the instrument and be in the same key.
But now what you're telling me now is a little bit different in the sense that why did the Spirits sing in those keys?
Because that's the way they did it.
They learned them in the concert keys.
And also probably maybe their vocals were --
You could hear the vocals in those keys.
